The historian D. A. Khozhaev wrote: "On arriving in Tiflis, Beibulat learns that Paskevich is with the army in the field. Realizing that he has been deceived, he tries to return to Chechnya immediately, but he is forcibly detained in Tiflis"[1]. Paskevich admitted the deception in his own hand in his instruction to Emanuel of August 2, 1829: "I at once resolved to summon to myself, under the guise of explanations, their elders and the elder Bei-Bulat known to you, so that, having drawn them away here, I might deprive this tribe of the possibility, in case of discontent, of undertaking anything hostile"[2]. |
| **[T0099 Hostage-Taking January 1828 C1150 Deception and Forcible Detention of Beibulat Taimiev by Paskevich, Splitting Chechnya into Factions, and Coercion into an Oath of Allegiance (1828-1829) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0099Hostage-Taking)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/361):** From spring until the end of summer 1829, Commander-in-Chief Paskevich forcibly kept with the field army the Chechen elders who had been summoned for negotiations, directly calling them hostages. In his instruction to Emanuel of May 16, 1829, he wrote: "The mere absence of these people, who will be with us in the manner of amanats, will restrain the unpacified Chechens from any hostile attempts"[2]. He summed up the result on August 2, 1829: "The Chechen elders, having been graciously received by me, remained with the detachment and were with me in military operations against the Turks. Having kept them in this way for a whole summer, I secured tranquility for the Line on their part"[2]. By the same document, hostage-taking was entrenched as a system of governing Chechnya: "As a pledge of the submission of the said Chechens, the amanats presented by each eldership are to be kept in the fortress of Grozny; and if from any one an amanat has not yet been delivered, then the elder, until the amanat is delivered, is obliged... to remain himself as a pledge in the fortress of Grozny"[2]. |
| **[T0038 Economic Control January 1828 C1150 Deception and Forcible Detention of Beibulat Taimiev by Paskevich, Splitting Chechnya into Factions, and Coercion into an Oath of Allegiance (1828-1829) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0038Economic Control)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/343):** By the regulation of August 2, 1829, Commander-in-Chief Paskevich locked the Chechens' access to trade onto a commissar appointed by the empire: travel to imperial territory was permitted only with tickets — "To him is also granted the right to issue tickets to the said Chechens for travel into our domains on trade business"[2]. In practice, the pass system was supplemented by arbitrariness: Chechen society wrote to Paskevich on November 21, 1829 that Engelhardt and Khasai-Musa "order their subordinates to place under arrest all those Chechens who come to them with tickets from Shahbaz," while those obedient to Khasai-Musa act so that the Chechens are deprived of their "means of sustenance"[2]. |

</details>

posts.title: Instrumentalization of a Natural Disaster by the Colonizers: Paskevich and Rosen Declare the Earthquake "God's Punishment of the Nokhchi People for Disobedience to the Empire" (1830)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Instrumentalization of a Natural Disaster by the Colonizers: Paskevich and Rosen Declare the Earthquake "God's Punishment of the Nokhchi People for Disobedience to the Empire" (1830) (C1151)

At the end of February 1830, the Caucasus was struck by a devastating earthquake that lasted more than a month and caused panic among the mountain peoples. The empire turned the disaster into a weapon of indoctrination and delivered this lie to the people. The historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov wrote: "supporters of the Russian orientation claimed that the earthquake had been caused by the wrath of Allah over the attempt at an armed uprising"[1]. The mechanics of the indoctrination are acknowledged by the colonizers themselves. The imperial historian Volkonsky wrote: "the commander-in-chief accordingly ordered General Rosen 4th to spread entirely opposite rumors among the people, namely, that the earthquake had been sent down by God upon the mountain peoples for their ill-intentioned acts against the Russian government, and hoped by this means to tear his followers away from Kazi-Mulla"[2]. The imperial historian Potto admits that the order was carried out: General Rosen 4th, who commanded the troops on the left flank of the Caucasus Line (the eastern section of the empire's fortified frontier along the Terek and the Sunzha), "resorted to proclamations in which he strove to assure the people that the earthquake had been sent down upon them as punishment for their treason and ill-intentioned acts against the Russian government"[3].

---

<details><summary>**Procedures Carried Out (1)**</summary>

| Procedures Carried Out |
|---|
| **[T0007 Imposition of Its Own Picture of Reality January 1830 C1151 Instrumentalization of a Natural Disaster by the Colonizers: Paskevich and Rosen Declare the Earthquake "God's Punishment of the Nokhchi People for Disobedience to the Empire" (1830) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0007Imposition of Its Own Picture of Reality)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/317):** In 1830, during an ongoing earthquake, General Rozen 4th, who commanded the troops on the left flank of the Caucasus Line (the eastern section of the empire's fortified border along the Terek and Sunzha rivers), on the orders of commander-in-chief Paskevich sent proclamations out to the auls, instilling in the people an artificial picture of the world: the natural disaster was declared God's punishment for resisting the empire. The historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov wrote about how this lie sounded among the Nokhchi: "supporters of the Russian orientation claimed that the earthquake was caused by the wrath of Allah over the attempt at an armed uprising"[1]. The imperial historian Volkonsky acknowledges the source of the suggestion: the commander-in-chief "ordered General Rozen 4th to spread entirely opposite rumors among the people, namely, that the earthquake had been sent down by God upon the Mountain Peoples for their ill-intentioned acts against the Russian government"[2]. The imperial historian Potto recorded the act: Rozen "resorted to proclamations in which he sought to assure the people that the earthquake had been sent down upon them as punishment for their treason and their ill-intentioned acts against the Russian government"[3]. |

</details>

posts.title: Burning of Lowland Chechnya by Velyaminov's Expedition: Demolition of Villages from the Sunzha to Mairtup, Seizure of Astemir's Family, Collective Penalties Imposed on Chechen Villages, the Cutting Down of Fleeing Inhabitants of Dzulgai-Yurt, and Destruction of Winter Stores (1830-1831)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Burning of Lowland Chechnya by Velyaminov's Expedition: Demolition of Villages from the Sunzha to Mairtup, Seizure of Astemir's Family, Collective Penalties Imposed on Chechen Villages, the Cutting Down of Fleeing Inhabitants of Dzulgai-Yurt, and Destruction of Winter Stores (1830-1831) (C1152)

In the fall of 1830, General Velyaminov, who had taken command of the troops operating against Chechnya, began with collective property exactions from the Chechen villages standing on the Terek River near the imperial border. The imperial historian Potto admits: for the driving off by Chechens of ten head of cattle from the stanitsa of Chervlennaya, Velyaminov "immediately ordered that ten head of cattle likewise be taken from the inhabitants of the two villages of Braguny and Novy-Yurt, past which the raiding party had gone, and returned to the Cossacks," and after a herd of horses was driven off in the Nogai steppe, "Braguny again paid with exactly the same number of head"; the owner of Novy-Yurt, Shah-Girei, was summoned to Groznaya and confined in a casemate — a prison cell inside the fortress[1]. On December 18, 1830, a detachment assembled in Groznaya consisting of four infantry regiments — the Moscow, Butyrsky, Tarutino, and Borodino regiments — a composite battalion of the 43rd Jaeger Regiment, five sotnias of line Cossacks, and twenty-two guns, and at night the troops moved on the village of Dzulgai-Yurt, where the Karabulak leader Astemir lived. Potto wrote: the Cossacks, bursting into the village at dawn, rushed to Astemir's house; he himself managed to escape, "but his family — a young son, a daughter, a grandson, and a female cousin — fell into the hands of the Cossacks. Besides them, thirty-nine people were taken prisoner, and about twelve were cut down"[1]. Then the villages of western, Lesser Chechnya were destroyed one after another: Kiter-Yurt "was given over to the flames," Pkhan-Kichu was burned down, at the village of Daut-Martan "the inhabitants managed to flee, but all their property remained the booty of the detachment," Edin-Yurt and Daut-Yurt were burned, "enormous stores of harvested hay" were destroyed, Martan-aul and Dzhargan-Yurt were occupied, the aul of Engeli was exterminated[1]. Between campaigns, the troops cut a clearing through the forest between the village of Aldy and the fortress of Groznaya. In January 1831 the blow was shifted to eastern, Greater Chechnya: Uzeken-Yurt was burned, Besenber with all its hamlets was destroyed. The villages of Avtury, Geldigen, and Mairtup sent their elders with an offer of submission and hostages, but Velyaminov rejected them, demanding the surrender of all Russian captives and deserter soldiers. The condition was a double impossibility, and Potto himself deciphers this: they "could not have had many" captives — captives did not settle in the villages but left through exchange and ransom, which both sides practiced; as for deserters, the Nokhchi did not hand them over — the Chechens, by Potto's admission, "regarded them... as men who had given themselves under the protection of their hearths, and therefore never surrendered them"[1]. Hospitality is a value celebrated in Chechen illi (heroic songs) on a par with courage and fidelity to one's word, and handing over a fugitive meant sending a guest to his death: the historian D. A. Khozhaev wrote of the marching gallows "on which the general [Yermolov] hanged highlanders and fugitive Russian soldiers and Cossacks who were hiding in mountain auls," and recorded that the demand for "the surrender of fugitive Russian soldiers and Cossacks living in the mountain auls" was a constant instrument of the imperial bailiffs (pristavs)[2]. By demanding simultaneously the nonexistent and the inadmissible, Velyaminov engineered a refusal: "this belated and forced submission was not at all part of Velyaminov's designs; he understood the necessity of punishing these auls cruelly, and perhaps that is why he set before them conditions which, in the view of the highlanders, were unthinkable"[1]. Avtury was taken by storm and burned, Geldigen was consigned to the flames with all its stores, and on January 21 Mairtup "with its luxuriant gardens and plantations" was destroyed together with the surrounding auls[1]. Potto sums up the result with an admission: "all of lowland Chechnya, traversed through and through as far as the Kochalykovsky ridge, was given over by Velyaminov to fire and sword"[1].

---

The imperial historian Potto wrote of the method: Velyaminov "would usually mark out a point toward which he advanced unswervingly with his entire detachment, and then, upon reaching it, immediately set up camp and established a fortified wagenburg (a camp enclosed by wagons), from which the troops were dispatched in turn in small columns to exterminate the neighboring auls"[1]. The imperial historian Potto wrote: "his family — a young son, a daughter, a grandson, and a cousin — fell into the hands of the Cossacks. Besides them, thirty-nine people were taken prisoner"[1]. |

This was recorded by the imperial historian Potto[1]. |
| **[T0121 Artificial Famine September 1830 C1152 Burning of Lowland Chechnya by Velyaminov's Expedition: Demolition of Villages from the Sunzha to Mairtup, Seizure of Astemir's Family, Collective Penalties Imposed on Chechen Villages, the Cutting Down of Fleeing Inhabitants of Dzulgai-Yurt, and Destruction of Winter Stores (1830-1831) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0121Artificial Famine)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/393):** In December 1830 – January 1831, General Velyaminov's troops deliberately destroyed the winter stores of food and fodder of the villages being devastated. The imperial historian Potto wrote: during the burning of Edin-Yurt and Daut-Yurt, the troops "destroyed enormous stores of harvested hay"[1]; on January 17, 1831, Geldigen was put to the torch "with all its stores"[1]. The destruction of hay and grain stores in the depths of winter condemned the inhabitants, who had fled to the mountains and forests, to famine. |

The imperial historian Potto wrote: Velyaminov "set about cutting a clearing and clearing a road between Aldy and Groznaya in order to prepare for himself a secure gateway to the south"[1]. On January 21, 1831, Mairtup was exterminated "with its luxuriant gardens and plantations" — orchards of many years' standing, the foundation of the village's way of life, were destroyed[1]. |

posts.title: Assassination of Chechen resistance leader Beibulat Taimiev, prepared by the imperial command (1831)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Assassination of Chechen resistance leader Beibulat Taimiev, prepared by the imperial command (1831) (C1153)

After his escape from surveillance in the fall of 1830, the leader of the Chechen resistance Beibulat Taimiev — bound by his oath to Paskevich, by fractures of both legs, and by illness — took no part in hostilities, but his name alone inspired the insurgents. The historian D. A. Khozhaev wrote: "The tsarist command several times intended to do away with Beibulat, but feared to repress him openly, since this could provoke an undesirable resonance throughout Chechnya. And yet the continued presence of a man like Beibulat in insurgent Chechnya was becoming dangerous for the tsarist command. Preparations began for the murder of Beibulat, which was soon carried out"[1]. On July 14, 1831, not far from the fortification of Tashkichu, Beibulat was killed from ambush by Prince Sali, who was in imperial service. D. A. Khozhaev recorded the official version — the murder was presented as a blood feud — and its exposure: "Prince Sali, who was in tsarist service, was not punished, whereas the other cases of blood vengeance were cruelly prosecuted by the tsarist command. Paskevich wrote of the slain Beibulat that he had been a traitor to the end, and that therefore the killer should not be punished"[1].

---

posts.title: Velyaminov's winter raids on Chechen hamlets and villages along the Sunzha: capture of women and devastation of homesteads (1831-1832)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Velyaminov's winter raids on Chechen hamlets and villages along the Sunzha: capture of women and devastation of homesteads (1831-1832) (C1154)

In December 1831, General Velyaminov, without disbanding the detachment encamped near the fortress of Groznaya, switched to a tactic of raids on Chechen settlements. The imperial historian Volkonsky wrote: Velyaminov "decided to harass the enemy and divert his attention from our borders. Thus, on December 23, 1831, he sent on a raid the commander of the Mozdok Cossack Regiment, Lieutenant Colonel Zass, who devastated several Chechen hamlets on the right side of the Sunzha, lying opposite the village of Chertugai, and delivered to the camp three captive women and up to 250 head of cattle. In this raid the enemy left 7 bodies on the spot"[1]. In February 1832 the raiding tactic grew into an expedition through the villages standing along the Sunzha River above the fortress of Groznaya. The imperial review of military operations admits: "Lieutenant General Velyaminov in February 1832 undertook an expedition to punish the Chechen villages lying up the Sunzha from the fortress of Groznaya"[2]. The historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov wrote of the same strike: "Another large expedition was directed against the Chechen auls located along the banks of the Sunzha"[3].

posts.title: Extermination of 61 settlements of lowland Chechnya and mountainous Ichkeria by Rosen's troops, burning alive of the defenders of Germenchuk, and extortion of hostages from 80 villages (1832)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Extermination of 61 settlements of lowland Chechnya and mountainous Ichkeria by Rosen's troops, burning alive of the defenders of Germenchuk, and extortion of hostages from 80 villages (1832) (C1155)

In August 1832, corps commander Rosen led a ten-thousand-strong detachment on a campaign through Chechnya and Ichkeria — the mountainous southeastern part of Chechen land, into which imperial troops had never before penetrated. The historian D. A. Khozhaev wrote: "Rosen's ten-thousand-strong tsarist detachment invaded mountainous Ingushetia and Chechnya, ablaze with the fire of a people's war of liberation. Despite the steadfast resistance of the inhabitants of mountainous Chechnya, who courageously defended every inch of their land, the tsarist troops destroyed several dozen auls and hamlets"[1]. On August 22, after crossing the Argun River, the villages of Belgatoy and Dzhan-yurt were annihilated. On August 23, Germenchuk — the richest village of Chechnya, numbering 600 households — was taken by storm. Rosen reported to Minister of War Chernyshev: "more than 100 bodies were left by them in the village itself," while a group "numbering about 60 men, for the most part people sent by Kazi-Mulla to hearten the inhabitants of Germenchuk," led by Mullah Abdurakhman, "was cut off and surrounded by us in one large house"[2]. The surrounded men refused to surrender and, on the order of General Volkhovsky, were burned alive. The imperial historian Volkonsky, writing from Rosen's dispatches, admits: "Major General Volkhovsky ordered burning firewood and hay to be thrown into the chimneys. This had its effect... but the greater part, together with Mullah Abdurakhman, perished in the flames, continuing to sing verses of the Quran"[3]. For two days "the troops annihilated the houses of the village of Germenchuk"; on August 26, Shali was destroyed "with the exception of 11 households that had paid the fine and the tribute"[3]. Rosen himself acknowledged the pattern of the campaign: the villages, "having been unable to agree among themselves on the release of our prisoners, were punished by the annihilation of their dwellings and plowlands, for which purpose, on the 27th and 28th of this past August, Colonel Shumsky was dispatched... He annihilated Alkhan-yurt, Sala-yurt, Katar-yurt, Lyalsin-yurt, Nazari-yurt, Uzden-yurt, Uruzbey-yurt, and Khyzin-Erzo-yurt"[2]. Further annihilated were Anzeli-yurt and Chingaroy-yurt, the crops and dwellings of Avtury, Said-yurt, the plowlands and houses of Geldigen, Anto-yurt, Askhor-yurt, Taba-yurt, and Kudish-yurt; Mairtup was burned, and in Ichkeria — Shoni, Tsentoroy, Belgatoy, the hamlet of Khamer, Ali-yurt, Bey-Bulat-yurt, Bachin-yurt, Khelboyn-yurt; Benoy was burned[3][2][1]. Rosen summed up the results in his report to Chernyshev of September 27, 1832: "In all, up to the present time, more than 80 Chechen and Ichkerian villages have submitted, a quarter of which had never been in dependence on us; 30 of our prisoners, men and women, have been returned; tribute and fines in money and livestock have been paid... about 5 th. r. s. [five thousand rubles in silver]. 61 unsubmitted villages have been annihilated, many of which, after punishment, declared their submission and fulfilled all demands"[2].

The imperial historian Volkonsky wrote: "one woman was taken prisoner"[3]. posts.title: Covert reconnaissance of Chechnya by Rosen's topographers and the devastation of Zandak by Pullo's detachment: capture of 31 inhabitants and seizure of livestock (1835-1836)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Covert reconnaissance of Chechnya by Rosen's topographers and the devastation of Zandak by Pullo's detachment: capture of 31 inhabitants and seizure of livestock (1835-1836) (C1156)

In 1835–1836 the empire combined systematic punitive expeditions in Chechnya with covert reconnaissance of the territory. Corps commander Rosen, in a report to the emperor, admits the practice of clandestine study of unsubdued lands: the undertakings "consisted either in the collection of topographical information... or in covert surveys of the lands of the mountaineers hostile to us"; "in 1836, to survey the direct route leading from Kakheti to Chechnya, a topographer was sent, who, having crossed the snowy ridge, came out onto the Caucasian Line at the fortress of Groznaya, and from there, through Chechnya and the lands of the Kists and the Didoi, returned to Kakheti"; at the same time "I sent from Vladikavkaz Ensign Prince Utsmiev of the Life Guards Grenadier Regiment with a topographer, through Chechnya, to Andia"[1]. Against the movement of Imam Tashu-Hajji, Colonel Pullo, commander of the Sunzha fortified line, conducted constant expeditions; the imperial review of military operations admits: Tashu-Hajji's attempts "were forestalled in good time by the expeditions of the commander of the Sunzha Line, Colonel Pullo, which inflicted total ruin on the inhabitants"[1]. On August 23, 1836, Pullo's detachment, in a covert night march, reached the aul of Zandak on the Yaman-su River, where Tashu-Hajji was staying. Rosen reported to the minister of war: Pullo, "in order to shake the influence of Tashev-Hajji, to quell the unrest among the Chechens, and to instill fear in them, resolved to undertake movements to punish the inhabitants of the village of Zandak"; "the sudden appearance of our troops struck terror into the inhabitants"; the infantry, having driven out the defenders, seized "31 souls of male and female sex as prisoners. In addition, the property of the inhabitants and 384 head of horned cattle fell to our troops as booty"; before the withdrawal, the houses of the murids and of "other principal adherents of Tashev-Hajji" were annihilated[1]. The Chechen writer Abuzar Aydamirov, in his "Chronology of the History of Checheno-Ingushetia," recorded: "Punitive expedition of Colonel Pullo to the auls on the Yaman-Su River. Destruction of the aul of Zandak. Retreat of Pullo's detachment, under the pressure of Tashav-Hajji, to the fortress of Vnezapnaya"[2].

posts.title: Coercion of Devastated Zandak into Subordination and Tribute by Colonel Pullo (1836)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Coercion of Devastated Zandak into Subordination and Tribute by Colonel Pullo (1836) (C1157)

On 23 August 1836, the detachment of Colonel Pullo devastated the aul of Zandak on the Yaman-su river, taking inhabitants captive and driving away livestock (campaign C1156). The village's subordination was engineered by the devastation itself: Pullo calculatedly left some of the houses unburned so that the crushed village would have somewhere to return to beg for "submission". In a report to General Petrov dated 27 August 1836 he admitted: "Being certain that the inhabitants of Zandak, following the common custom of the Chechens, would ask for submission after punishment, and considering such submission useful for the government, I did not order the village burned"[1]. The same report recorded the mechanism of coercion: the devastation of Zandak, which had been considered impregnable, "brought both the inhabitants of the village and all those living in its vicinity into fear and despondency"[1]. Under this fear, as early as 27 August 1836 the elders of the devastated village came to the Groznaya fortress with a forced plea to be accepted into subjecthood; Rozen reported to the Minister of War: "On 27 August the Zandak elders appeared before the commander of the Sunzha Line declaring their submission, which was accepted from them in the established order"[2]. "Submission" was accepted only on the empire's terms: loyalty, a complete break with Tashu-Hadji, the leader of the Chechen resistance, a ban on assemblies, the handover of Russian captives in exchange for the inhabitants of Zandak seized by the troops during the devastation of the village, and payment of tribute at the rate established by the empire for the societies it deemed "submissive". Pullo enumerated: the people of Zandak "pledge for the time to come to remain loyal to us, allowing the inhabitants not the slightest contact with Tashav-Hadji... not to permit rebellious gatherings among themselves, to deliver our captives in exchange for their own taken during the devastation of Zandak, and to pay, on a par with the Aukhovites and other submissive tribes, the established tribute"[1]. Pullo assessed the outcome as the conqueror's gain: "All the above-stated consequences arising from the devastation of the Zandak people have produced important advantages for us"[1].

---

The subordination was engineered by the devastation itself: in a report to General Petrov dated 27 August 1836, Pullo admitted: "Being certain that the inhabitants of Zandak, following the common custom of the Chechens, would ask for submission after punishment, and considering such submission useful for the government, I did not order the village burned"[1]. The same report recorded the state in which the village went to its subordination: the devastation "brought both the inhabitants of the village and all those living in its vicinity into fear and despondency"[1]. The elders sent "a plea to be accepted into submission to the Russian government", and subjecthood was formalized on terms dictated by the empire: loyalty, a complete break with Tashu-Hadji, the leader of the Chechen resistance, a ban on assemblies, the handover of Russian captives in exchange for the inhabitants of Zandak seized during the devastation, and the established tribute[1]. Rozen recorded the fact and the date of the formalization in a dispatch to the Minister of War: "On 27 August the Zandak elders appeared before the commander of the Sunzha Line declaring their submission, which was accepted from them in the established order"[2]. |

In a report to General Petrov dated 27 August 1836, Pullo recorded the obligation accepted by the elders at the Groznaya fortress: "to pay, on a par with the Aukhovites and other submissive tribes, the established tribute"[1]. The tribute was not the village's counter-offer but the empire's standing norm for taxing the societies it deemed "submissive"; refusal would have meant the return of the "avenging arms of the Russians" - the village had just survived devastation, the captivity of its inhabitants, and the seizure of its livestock[1]. |

posts.title: Extermination of the Inhabitants of Kishkeroy-Yurt by Pullo's Detachment: 76 Killed, 40 Captured, Village Burned with Its Stores (December 1836)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Extermination of the Inhabitants of Kishkeroy-Yurt by Pullo's Detachment: 76 Killed, 40 Captured, Village Burned with Its Stores (December 1836) (C1158)

In late December 1836, Colonel Pullo, in a covert winter raid, exterminated the Chechen village of Kishkeroy-Yurt (Keshkeroy) beyond the Gudermes river. Sanction had been given in advance: on 10 December 1836 Rozen reported to the Minister of War Chernyshev that he "had authorized Col. Pullo to act at once against the unsubmissive Chechen villages"[1]. The pretext for the punishment was declared to be hospitality: the village's inhabitants "had harbored the rebel Tashov-Hadji"[2]. Surrounded at dawn, the village was exterminated together with its people: those fleeing "were caught or exterminated", while "the inhabitants, having barricaded themselves in their houses with their families, were put to the bayonet"[2]; an attempt by Tashu-Hadji to come to the village's relief was repelled by artillery. Rozen himself summed up the outcome: "Upon the occupation of the village of Kishkeroy-Yurt, 76 bodies of the slain were found in it, and 40 souls of both sexes were taken captive; all the property of the inhabitants and the weapons taken from the slain fell to our troops"[2][3]. The village of 63 households, "with a considerable stock of grain and hay," was put to the torch in the middle of winter[2]. Dating: the dispatch is dated in the collection "9 January 1836," but the compilers placed it among documents from late 1836 to early 1837; the raid almost certainly took place on 27-31 December 1836, while the historian Sh. A. Gapurov dates it to December 1835[3].

---

posts.title: Failed Attempt at Religious Subjugation of the Highlanders to the Empire through the Hiring of the Preacher Taj ad-Din Mustafin (1836-1841)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Failed Attempt at Religious Subjugation of the Highlanders to the Empire through the Hiring of the Preacher Taj ad-Din Mustafin (1836-1841) (C1159)

In 1836, the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps under General Rozen put forward a project to subordinate the entire Sunni clergy of the Caucasus to a "spiritual leader" appointed by the empire: for this role they hired the Kazan efendi (Muslim theologian) Taj ad-Din Mustafin and kept him on the treasury's payroll for about six years. The preacher's task was formulated openly: "to turn the highlanders onto the true path, subordinate them to the Russian government, and destroy or hand over Shamil to us alive" (Shamil - imam, leader of the Dagestani and Chechen highlanders' resistance to the Russian conquest)[1]. In Chechnya, Mustafin was sent to the Groznaya fortress to undermine the spiritual influence of Tashu-Hadji (sheikh, imam of Chechnya in 1834-1836, spiritual and military leader of the Chechen resistance). After a letter from Tashu-Hadji, who under threat of death forbade the preacher to appear on Chechen land, he acted only under military escort and did not show himself in the mountains. The project failed: Golovin, who succeeded Rozen, agreed to release the preacher based on a report by Minister of War Chernyshev of 13 November 1841 - "the teaching of Tajudin Effendi over the course of 6 years did not change the highlanders' attitude toward us in the slightest"[1].

---

The historian N. I. Pokrovsky wrote: "a broad project emerges for subordinating the entire mountain Sunni clergy to a special spiritual person"; the task set was "to turn the highlanders onto the true path, subordinate them to the Russian government, and destroy or hand over Shamil to us alive"[1]. Only the establishment of the post, the appointment, and the preacher's years-long payment took place; subordinating the clergy did not succeed: "The preacher did not dare to show himself in the mountains"[1]. The empire wound down the project only six years later: Golovin, who succeeded Rozen, agreed to release Mustafin based on a report by Minister of War Chernyshev of 13 November 1841 - "the teaching of Tajudin Effendi over the course of 6 years did not change the highlanders' attitude toward us in the slightest"[1]. |

The goal was stated in the source: "with the aim of undermining the spiritual influence" of Tashu-Hadji "and reducing the effectiveness of the preaching of ghazawat" (ghazawat - the highlanders' war for independence from the Russian conquest)[2]. The agent "had managed to make a trip to the lowland societies of Dagestan" when Tashu-Hadji, by letter, "under threat of death forbade him to appear on Chechen territory"[2]; the response is cited by the historian Pokrovsky: "I instruct you that you shall not travel about in these lands without our permission, and if you are not foolish, you should withdraw before harm is done to you"[1]. |

posts.title: Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) (C1160)

On 23-29 January 1837, the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps sent from the Groznaya fortress into Lesser Chechnya (the lowland-piedmont western part of Chechnya) a detachment under General Feze - 3249 men with 12 guns. Rozen stated the purpose of the campaign in a report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 11 February 1837: "to punish the Chechens of the western part of Chechnya who have evaded obedience"[1]. The expedition journal appended to the report records the week day by day: on the night of 24 January Shalazh-yurt was surrounded - the village was taken "without a shot, laying 14 souls on the spot", 67 inhabitants were led away into captivity, and the village was burned; on 25 January Feze dispatched columns "to discover and destroy the population in the dense forests up both banks of the Shalazha river"; in all, 92 people were taken captive over the campaign, "on the way back more than a thousand saklias were burned along the Martan and Tengin gorges" (saklia - a highlander's house), and the stores of grain and hay were destroyed in the middle of winter[1]. Within the detachment the empire led highlanders against highlanders - 800 horsemen of the Ossetian and Ingush militia (militia - auxiliary units of highlanders in the empire's service): the expedition journal lists in Colonel Shiroky's column "a hundred Cossacks and 800 horsemen of Ossetians and Ingush"[1]. From the aul of Achkhoy, which the troops entered on the fourth day of the annihilation of its neighbors, by the record of the same journal an oath "of submission" and six hostages-amanats were taken (amanat - a person whom the empire took from a community as a guarantee of subordination)[1].

---

Rozen, in a report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 11 February 1837, named the purpose plainly: "to punish the Chechens of the western part of Chechnya who have evaded obedience"[1]. The campaign continued the winter punitive operations after the December extermination of Kishkeroy-Yurt (campaign C1158): within a week, according to the expedition journal appended to the same report, Shalazh-yurt and the dwellings on both banks of the Shalazha were destroyed, more than a thousand saklias were burned, and 92 captives were taken[1]. |

On 25 January Feze, according to the same journal, dispatched columns "to discover and destroy the population in the dense forests up both banks of the Shalazha river" - an order for the destruction of the population in so many words[1]. The expedition journal, presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837, records: "Having burned Shalazh-yurt", the troops "destroyed the winter quarters... and the dwellings of the Chechens on both banks of the Shalazha", and "on the way back more than a thousand saklias were burned along the Martan and Tengin gorges"[1]. |

The expedition journal, presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837, names the composition of Colonel Shiroky's column: "a hundred Cossacks and 800 horsemen of Ossetians and Ingush" (the Ossetian and Ingush militia - auxiliary units of highlanders in the empire's service)[1]. The use of neighboring peoples in a punitive campaign shifted part of the suppression onto the colonized themselves and entrenched enmity between them. |

The frame is spelled out by the expedition journal itself, presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837: "the troops are proceeding to them not to punish them, but properly to confirm them in submission"[1] - subordination secured under military pressure and framed by the empire as a voluntary act of those who had submitted. |

posts.title: Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) (C1161)

In February-April 1837, the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps conducted a series of expeditions under General Feze across Chechnya, coercing community after community into an oath to the empire. Rozen stated the sanction in a dispatch to Minister of War Chernyshev: a campaign "beyond the Argun" would be useful "for diminishing the Chechens' trust in the instigators and turning them away from the intention of joining Shamil" (Shamil - imam, leader of the Dagestani and Chechen highlanders' resistance to the Russian conquest)[1]. Rozen's reports to Chernyshev describe the mechanism themselves: after the annihilation of the auls of Akhoy-yurt, Lyumik-yurt, Seid-yurt and Avtur, "the Chechens, gripped by fear from the preceding actions... fell into great despondency" - and the troops took oaths with amanats (amanat - a person whom the empire took from a community as a guarantee of subordination) from Shali on 6 February, Germenchuk on the 8th, Geldigen on the 15th, six auls of the Michik on the 21st, the auls along the Yaman-su and the Aksai on the 25th, and, at the end of March, from the elders of the Goyta forest and the Martan gorge[1]. The summary in the report of 4 March 1837 counts, for eleven February days: "52 souls of inhabitants who did not submit voluntarily were taken captive by our troops... and 52 amanats were taken"[1]. General Feze stated the calculation openly - he acted "with the intention of making use, as far as possible, of the panic fear" (report to Velyaminov of 15 March 1837)[2]. In March the troops passed up the Dzhalka: "the four auls they had abandoned were occupied and annihilated without resistance", and the kutans (winter shelters for livestock) with their grain stores were destroyed[1]. At the end of April a night raid on the Gertli settlement took "18 souls belonging to the families of the brigands" and 465 head of livestock, and "a fine of 132 head of livestock was imposed on the settlement"[1]. The voice of the Nokhchi records the tour as an invasion - the historian D. A. Khozhaev writes: "at the end of February-beginning of March the enemy again invaded Ichkeria. On 1 March, at the village of Aleroy, a battle took place between the detachment of Tashu-Hadji's companion Udi-mullah and the troops of General Fezi" (Tashu-Hadji - sheikh, imam of Chechnya in 1834-1836, spiritual and military leader of the Chechen resistance)[3].

---

<details><summary>**Procedures Carried Out (11)**</summary>

| Procedures Carried Out |
|---|
| **[T0077 Punitive Expeditions February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0077Punitive Expeditions)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/359):** In February-April 1837, continuing the January annihilation of Lesser Chechnya (campaign C1160), the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps conducted a series of expeditions under General Feze across eastern and central Chechnya: the February movement through Shali, Germenchuk and the Michik, the March march up the Dzhalka, and the April night raid on the Gertli settlement. Rozen set out the sanction in a dispatch to Minister of War Chernyshev: a campaign "beyond the Argun" - "for diminishing the Chechens' trust in the instigators and turning them away from the intention of joining Shamil"[1]. The Gertli raid was declared a punishment in Rozen's report to Chernyshev of 30 May 1837: "for the devastation or final annihilation of this brigand party... and for the punishment of its inhabitants"[1]. |
| **[T0022 Terror February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0022Terror)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/330):** Feze's spring tour across Chechnya was built on demonstrative violence converted into submission. Rozen's report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 4 March 1837 records the result of the annihilation of the auls: "the Chechens, gripped by fear from the preceding actions... fell into great despondency"[1] - after which the oaths followed one after another. Feze himself reported the calculation to General Velyaminov on 15 March 1837: he acted "with the intention of making use, as far as possible, of the panic fear" that had gripped "the Tavlins and the Andians" after the battle at Avtury[2]; Rozen's report of 11 March uses the same word for the demand of submission from the Andians - "wishing to make use of the fear"[1]. Fear drove people off their land: after the March sweeps through the forests the inhabitants, according to the report of 12 April, "were compelled by these searches to withdraw into the distant mountains"[1]. |
| **[T0147 Forced Registration of Subjecthood February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0147Forced Registration of Subjecthood)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/417):** In February-March 1837, Feze's troops, annihilating the auls of those who evaded, took oaths to the empire from the Chechen communities one after another - Rozen's reports to Minister of War Chernyshev count them by date: on 6 February Shali ("brought an oath of submission to our government and presented amanats as its pledge"), on 8 February Germenchuk ("the oath of subjecthood was renewed"), on 15 February Geldigen ("brought an oath of allegiance and handed over amanats chosen from the best families"), on 21 February six auls of the Michik, on 25 February the auls along the Yaman-su from Balan-su to Biletli and on the Aksai[1]. By 24 February, according to the report of 11 March, Feze "brought to submission the Chechens dwelling along the Michik river"; at the end of March, at the camp at Ustar-khan, the troops took an oath from the elders of the Goyta forest and the Martan gorge - they "brought an oath of allegiance to the Sovereign Emperor and presented amanats as security for their submission"[1]. An oath taken under the guns of troops that had just annihilated the neighboring auls fixed subordination as a legal fact. |
| **[T0099 Hostage-Taking February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0099Hostage-Taking)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/361):** Every oath of Feze's spring tour was paid for in people: the troops took amanats from every community that submitted. Rozen's reports to Minister of War Chernyshev record the mechanism: Shali - "presented amanats as its pledge", Geldigen - "handed over amanats chosen from the best families", the Yaman-su and the Aksai - "with amanats as its security", the Goyta forest and the Martan gorge - "presented amanats as security for their submission"; the summary of 4 March 1837 counts: for 12-22 February "52 amanats were taken"[1]. In April, in the Gertli settlement, according to the report of 30 May, "Feze ordered the elder's family and 12 more souls to be taken into custody"[1]. |
| **[T0053 Abduction of People February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0053Abduction of People)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/354):** Over Feze's spring tour across Chechnya, the troops led away dozens of inhabitants into captivity, most of them unarmed. The summary in Rozen's report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 4 March 1837: for 12-22 February "52 souls of inhabitants who did not submit voluntarily were taken captive by our troops, including 8 armed men"[1] - that is, 44 of the 52 captives bore no arms. The report of 23 February on the burning of Seid-yurt and Avtur: "one Chechen and three women who had not managed to get away into the forest" were taken[1]. On the night of 22 March at Gurdali, according to the report of 12 April, Lieutenant Colonel Panteleyev "took captive 9 unsubmissive Chechens"; in the April raid on the Gertli settlement "18 more souls belonging to the families of the brigands were seized"[1]. |
| **[T0105 Total Destruction of Infrastructure February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0105Total Destruction of Infrastructure)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/366):** Feze's spring tour destroyed the housing and winter livelihood of the Chechen communities. Rozen's report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 23 February 1837: on 5 February "our troops annihilated the auls of Akhoy-yurt and Lyumik-yurt lying on the way and the khutors of the hostile Chechens"; on 9 February Seid-yurt and Avtur were annihilated[1]. In the March march up the Dzhalka, according to the report of 12 April, "the four auls they had abandoned were occupied and annihilated without resistance. Then the troops penetrated into the thick of the forest and destroyed the kutans"; on 26 March the troops were destroying kutans near Shali, and Birzul's column did the same along its own route[1]. |
| **[T0121 Artificial Famine February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0121Artificial Famine)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/393):** Destroying the kutans along the Dzhalka and near Shali in March 1837, Feze's troops deliberately burned food. Rozen's report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 12 April 1837 records: in the kutans they "burned a considerable quantity of the grain found in them"; near Shali the troops "seized the watchmen present at them and a multitude of food supplies"; and Birzul's column burned "several hundred chetverts of the grain found in them" (chetvert - an old grain measure of about 210 liters)[1]. Burning hundreds of chetverts of grain at the end of winter left the families who had fled to the forests and mountains without means to survive until the harvest. |
| **[T0164 Pillage February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0164Pillage)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/611):** Throughout Feze's spring tour, the troops took the Chechens' livestock and property. According to Rozen's reports to Minister of War Chernyshev: on 5 February the livestock of mullah Udi's detachment was taken - "148 head of livestock of various kinds"; on 11 February "213 head of livestock of various kinds belonging to the unsubmissive Chechens were seized"; against those hiding in the forests "searches were made in various directions... and livestock of various kinds and property were seized from many of them"[1]. The April raid on the Gertli settlement, according to the report of 30 May, took "465 head of small livestock"[1]. |
| **[T0140 Destruction of the Natural Landscape February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0140Destruction of the Natural Landscape)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/412):** Feze's spring tour cut military roads through the Chechen forests. According to Rozen's reports to Minister of War Chernyshev: in February a road was cut "in the forests through the Qachqalyq mountains along the Michik and between the auls of Kazbek and Aku-yurt"; the report of 12 April notes that the March march went "by the clearing cut by him in February of this year"; Feze himself moved at the end of February "working the pack trail into a road fit for the passage of all kinds of loads"[1]. Clearings and roads through the forests deprived the Chechen communities of their natural protection and opened the troops permanent access into the depth of the country. |
| **[T0057 Labor Exploitation February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0057Labor Exploitation)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/356):** The submission taken by Feze's troops in February 1837 immediately turned into labor duty. Rozen's report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 4 March 1837 records: on 21 February "the inhabitants of six neighboring auls declared their submission and sent out workers to cut, together with the Kumyks, a road in the forests through the Qachqalyq mountains along the Michik"[1] - communities just subordinated were set by the empire to cut the forest for a military road against themselves; the duty came as part of the package of submission, as the standard "Conditions Prescribed to Submitting Highlanders" would later codify it. |
| **[T0159 Collective Punishment February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0159Collective Punishment)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/603):** By the April 1837 raid on the Gertli settlement the troops of General Feze imposed a collective property levy on the whole village: according to Rozen's report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 30 May, on top of the livestock taken during the raid "a fine of 132 head of livestock was imposed on the settlement"[1] - the settlement paid as a whole, with no regard to the personal involvement of its residents. |

</details>

## List of Materials

1. [Кавказская археографическая комиссия. Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том VIII (1… 1881.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/105)
2. [Гаджиев В. Г., Рамазанов X. X. Движение горцев северо-восточного Кавказа в 20-50 гг. XIX века: сборник… 1959.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/126)
3. [Хожаев Д. А. Чеченцы в Русско-Кавказской войне. 1998.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/95)

---

posts.title: Attempted bribery of Shamil with a promise of power over Dagestan to secure his appearance before Nicholas I in Tiflis, and the summoning of the Chechen imam Tashu-Hadji (1837)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: Attempted bribery of Shamil with a promise of power over Dagestan to secure his appearance before Nicholas I in Tiflis, and the summoning of the Chechen imam Tashu-Hadji (1837) (C1162)

In September 1837, ahead of Nicholas I's visit to the Caucasus, the empire tried to buy the leader of the highlander resistance: Shamil (Shamil - imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest) was offered "pardon", honors and power in exchange for appearing before the emperor in Tiflis. General Adlerberg conveyed Nicholas I's will to general Rozen in a letter of 10 August 1837: "that Shamil and his chief accomplices Tashav-Hadji, Kibit-Magomet and the Qarakh qadi Abdurrahman be given suggestions to take advantage of His Majesty's arrival in the Caucasus region and to beg the mercy of appearing before the face of the Monarch Himself"[1] - Tashu-Hadji (sheikh, in 1834-1836 the imam of Chechnya, spiritual and military leader of the Chechen resistance) is named first among the "accomplices". General Klugenau obtained a personal meeting with Shamil on 18 September 1837 at a spring near the aul of Karanay; Shamil's chronicler Muhammad Tahir al-Qarakhi recorded the essence of the offer: "Kluki von Klugenau began to speak, asking Shamil to come for a meeting with the Russian Nicholas. He asserted that the emperor would exalt him, Shamil, show him honor, and make him the administrator of the affairs of all Dagestani Muslims. From the emperor, he said, there would be no treachery"[2]. At the same time colonel Pullo demanded of Shamil by letter that he send "to the Groznaya fortress two deputies to be presented to the Sovereign" - and this competing demand, as the imperial historian Yurov admits, "greatly hindered the success" of the recruitment[1]. Shamil refused in a letter to Klugenau of 28 September 1837: "I have resolved not to go to Tiflis even if I am cut to pieces, because I have many times seen treachery from you"[1] - neither he nor Tashu-Hadji appeared before the emperor.

---

<details><summary>**Procedures Carried Out (1)**</summary>

| Procedures Carried Out |
|---|
| **[T0015 Bribery of Elites September 1837 C1162 Attempted bribery of Shamil with a promise of power over Dagestan to secure his appearance before Nicholas I in Tiflis, and the summoning of the Chechen imam Tashu-Hadji (1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0015Bribery of Elites)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/324):** In September 1837, preparing Nicholas I's visit to the Caucasus, the empire tried to recruit Shamil, offering him power and honors in exchange for subordination to the empire. General Adlerberg conveyed the emperor's will to general Rozen in a letter of 10 August 1837: to give "Shamil and his chief accomplices Tashav-Hadji, Kibit-Magomet and the Qarakh qadi Abdurrahman suggestions... to beg the mercy of appearing before the face of the Monarch Himself" in Tiflis[1]; Tashu-Hadji is named first on the list. Carrying this out, general Klugenau obtained a personal meeting with Shamil on 18 September 1837 at a spring near the aul of Karanay; as recorded by Shamil's chronicler Muhammad Tahir al-Qarakhi, the general "began to speak, asking Shamil to come for a meeting with the Russian Nicholas. He asserted that the emperor would exalt him, Shamil, show him honor, and make him the administrator of the affairs of all Dagestani Muslims. From the emperor, he said, there would be no treachery"[2]. In parallel, general Feze instructed Akhmed Khan of Mekhtuli "to persuade Shamil to arrive in Tiflis by the time of His Majesty's arrival there", as general Rozen reported to Chernyshev on 25 September 1837[3], and colonel Pullo demanded of Shamil by letter that he send "to the Groznaya fortress two deputies to be presented to the Sovereign"[1]. The bribe was delivered to its addressee and rejected: on 28 September 1837 Shamil replied to Klugenau by letter - "I have resolved not to go to Tiflis even if I am cut to pieces, because I have many times seen treachery from you"[1]; neither Shamil nor Tashu-Hadji went to Tiflis. The offer to Shamil of the post of "administrator of the affairs of all Dagestani Muslims" repeated the same policy line by which the empire, in those same years, was creating loyal religious institutions (campaign C1159). |

</details>

## List of Materials

1. [Юров А. Три года на Кавказе (1837-1839). 1884.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/133)
2. [Мухаммад Тахир аль-Карахи. Блеск дагестанских шашек в некоторых шамилевских битвах. 1941.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/128)
3. [Кавказская археографическая комиссия. Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том VIII (1… 1881.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/105)

posts.title: The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) (C1163)

From September 1836 to February 1840 Pullo, commander of the Sunzha Line and then of the left flank of the Caucasus Line (a chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), built in the auls of Chechnya seized by the empire a system of coercion made of seven interlocking institutions: amanat hostages taken from the most respected families, a tribute of one silver ruble per saklia (house), pristavs - superintendents appointed by the empire, a ban on selling bread to the "nemirnye" (auls that had not submitted to the empire) and on pasturing their cattle on the plain, confiscation of weapons, forced felling of forests and clearings stretching 165 versts, and punishments "according to the degree of guilt" - up to the destruction of the villages themselves. Handing over the command, Pullo summed it up in a memorandum of 1840: "by threatening all the unsubmissive communities with the annihilation of their property, I instilled in them such fear, brought them to such a state, that one after another they began to submit"[1]. The system ended in an uprising. Hadji-Ali, a companion and chronicler of Shamil (Shamil - imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest), recorded: "As the oppressions of general Pullo over the Chechens intensified, so grew the requests of the latter to Shamil to come and free them"[2]. The imperial historian Yurov admitted both the cause and the culprit: "we ourselves assisted Shamil as only his true friends could have done"; "Rumors about the true causes of the uprising of Chechnya reached the attention of the Sovereign Emperor", after which general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line and Pullo's superior, deemed it necessary "to immediately remove, under a plausible pretext, major-general Pullo from the administration of the left flank"[3]. In February 1840 lowland Chechnya rose and called upon Shamil - the system collapsed together with the career of its builder.

---

<details><summary>**Procedures Carried Out (13)**</summary>

| Procedures Carried Out |
|---|
| **[T0099 Hostage-Taking September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0099Hostage-Taking)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/361):** In 1836-1840 Pullo, commander of the Sunzha Line and then of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, made hostage-taking the load-bearing institution of the amanat-and-tribute system in the auls of Chechnya seized by the empire. An amanat is a person whom the empire took away from a family or community as a hostage; the threat of reprisal against the taken one held the relatives and the whole aul in subjection. In a memorandum of 1840 Pullo described the method: "I took amanats not indiscriminately, as was done before, but from the most respected or least reliable families, and by this means many auls plotting revolt were repeatedly kept in obedience" - and the scale of the institution: "up to 20 thousand rubles... were spent yearly on the upkeep of amanats"[1]. The taking of hostages went in waves as the troops advanced: the imperial historian Yurov recorded of December 1839 that under the pressure of the detachment even the villages that barred the entrance to the Argun gorge "humbled themselves, handed over amanats" - the troops took people as a "token of submission"[3]. Yurov described the conditions in which the hostages were kept: "prisoners and even amanats were treated inhumanly, kept in a damp pit, where they often fell ill"[3]. In the same memorandum Pullo demanded that hostageship be made perpetual: for the offenses of those under warranty, amanats "must without fail, according to their age, be transferred into cantonists or convict companies, replacing the departed with other amanats" - child hostages to be handed into the cantonists (a military estate into which the empire forcibly enrolled minors), adults into convict companies (forced labor under military escort); in the memorandum of 1840 this is recorded as a plan[1]. |
| **[T0036 Installation of a New System of Governance September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0036Installation of a New System of Governance)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/341):** The empire placed appointed overseers - pristavs - over the seized auls of Chechnya. The empire's Minister of War Chernyshev, by an official communication of 15 January 1839, conveyed to general Golovin, commander of the Separate Caucasus Corps - the head of the empire's troops and administration in the Caucasus, the will of emperor Nicholas I: in the communities that submitted voluntarily, "the authority over them is to be entrusted to natives devoted to us, members of those same communities", while communities "that will be subjugated by force of arms" were "to be entrusted temporarily to the authority of Russian military officials"[4]. The pristavs in Chechnya were installed by Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line: the imperial historian Yurov writes that Pullo "was ordered - for the installation of our pristavs, to uphold their prestige at the outset... to carry out in the winter of 1839-1840 a movement into Chechnya, to the Michik and to the Qachqalyq people", and the pristavs themselves "were chosen predominantly, if not exclusively, from among the militiamen" - from the highland militia, armed units of highlanders in the empire's service[3]. The historian D. A. Khozhaev writes: "Appointed on 30 November commander of the Separate Caucasus Corps... Golovin, on the tsar's instruction, begins to introduce Russian administration on the occupied territory"[5]. The regime of surveillance was described by general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line and Pullo's superior, in a report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 23 March 1840: "When our pristavs entered upon the administration of the tribes entrusted to them, their strict surveillance cut off the constant relations of the peaceful auls with the unsubdued"[4]. The implanting of puppet religious authorities proceeded under the same directive (campaign C1159). |
| **[T0056 Taxation September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0056Taxation)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/355):** The amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, imposed a tribute on the seized auls of Chechnya. Pullo in a memorandum of 1840: "As the highland communities were subjugated, each handed over amanats, paid a tribute of one silver ruble per saklia, handed over all Russian captives held by it" (saklia - a highlander's house: the tribute was levied on every house; amanats - hostages whom the empire took away from the auls to control them)[1]. The 1840 register of the highland peoples, published in the documentary collection «Движение горцев северо-восточного Кавказа в 20-50 гг. XIX века» together with Pullo's memorandum, calls the tribute a punishment outright: the Qachqalyq people, the Michik Chechens and the Aukhovites (Chechen communities of eastern Chechnya) "pay a tribute imposed on them as punishment for repeated revolts", and the Chechens living beyond the Sunzha river, "as punishment for revolt, have been burdened with a tribute"[1]. The money was squeezed out regularly: general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line and Pullo's superior, in a report to the empire's Minister of War Chernyshev of 23 March 1840, named the regular payment of tributes a sign of the "tranquility" that had set in - the report lists the "regular payment of tributes and duties" weeks before the uprising[4]. Muhammad Tahir al-Qarakhi, the chronicler of Shamil, named this exaction - one ruble from every house and one gun from every ten houses - as the reason the Chechens called upon Shamil. |
| **[T0108 Economic Blockade September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0108Economic Blockade)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/368):** Part of the amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, was a regime of economic blockade of the auls of Chechnya that had not submitted. Pullo in a memorandum of 1840: the overseers appointed by the empire over the auls (the pristavs) and the troops "cut off the relations of the submitted with the unsubdued and forbade the former to sell bread to the nemirnye and to pasture their cattle on their fields" ("nemirnye" - in the imperial lexicon, auls that had not submitted to the empire)[1]. The permitted trade was driven under control: "In Kizlyar and at some other points trading fairs opened" - exchange took place only at points controlled by the empire[1]. The workings of the blockade were admitted by its own authors: general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line and Pullo's superior, in a report to the empire's Minister of War Chernyshev of 23 March 1840, wrote that the mountain auls "could no longer have tillage and pasture on the plain", which "further aggravated the distressed condition of the inhabitants of highland Chechnya"; some of the inhabitants thought of submitting "to avert famine", others resolved "to rid themselves of the Russian yoke"[4]. In a plan for the conquest of the highlanders of the left flank drawn up in 1840 (the "Proposition... for the subjugation of the tribes"), Grabbe formulated how the blockade worked: the pristavs' surveillance "threatened the unsubdued with famine. Shamil took advantage of this disposition of minds"[4]. |
| **[T0146 Administrative Corruption and Extortion September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0146Administrative Corruption and Extortion)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/416):** The overseers appointed by the empire over the auls, within the amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, systematically robbed the inhabitants of the seized auls of Chechnya under the guise of collections. The imperial historian Yurov described the mechanism - the pristavs lived off exactions, since "not all pristavs received a salary": from the Chechens, "under the pretext of collecting tributes and fines, the best weapons were taken away, and other entirely harmless but valuable articles of everyday use; it happened that people innocent of anything were arrested at the prompting of simple and often ill-intentioned interpreters... and during expeditions forced collections were permitted"[3]. The empire knew and would not listen: the historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write from archival documents that two Chechen elders brought to the Kabardian prince Bekovich-Cherkassky, who served the empire and was influential on the Terek river, "a petition drawn up on behalf of many Chechens, in which they complain of the oppressions and injustices of major-general Pullo" - the prince refused to accept the petition[6]; according to Yurov, the Chechens "had prepared a petition against him, but did not dare to set it in motion for fear that this general would remain their superior as before"[3]. The empire's survey "The Region in Political and Military Respects", sent by the empire's Minister of War Chernyshev to general Neidhardt, who soon headed the empire's troops in the Caucasus, on 2 April 1842, summed it up: "taking advantage of the abuses, the exactions and the indignation arising from the confiscation of weapons, Shamil little by little stirred all Chechnya to revolt"[7]. |
| **[T0057 Labor Exploitation September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0057Labor Exploitation)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/356):** The amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, included forced labor: the troops forced the inhabitants of the seized auls of Chechnya to fell their own forest by allotment. The imperial historian Yurov recorded of the December 1839 expedition that under the pressure of the detachment the inhabitants of the auls "felled forest by allotment at Gekhi, at the Valerik tract and between the villages of Shali and Malaya Ataga" (Gekhi, Valerik, Shali, Malaya Ataga - Chechen villages and tracts; "by allotment" - by a forced apportionment imposed by the troops alongside the tribute and the surrender of weapons)[3]. The forest the inhabitants were made to fell was the environment of life and the shelter of the Chechen communities. |
| **[T0140 Destruction of the Natural Landscape September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0140Destruction of the Natural Landscape)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/412):** Within the amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, the troops destroyed the Chechen forests - the environment of life and the protection of the Chechen communities. Pullo reported in a memorandum of 1840: "we cleared all the forests to the distance of a gunshot on both sides of the road, in the direction from the Groznaya fortress through Martan, Achkhoy and Kurchali to the Military-Georgian road, and in the other direction through Germenchuk, Geldygen and along the Michik into highland Chechnya, altogether over a stretch of 165 versts" (the listed names are Chechen villages and rivers from the Groznaya fortress to mountain Chechnya; a verst is slightly over a kilometer)[1]. The Chechen writer Abuzar Aydamirov records the continuation of the clearing (a strip cut through the forest for the passage of troops) from the Groznaya fortress toward the village of Shali in 1837[8]. |
| **[T0139 Construction of Fortresses September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0139Construction of Fortresses)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/411):** The amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, was anchored by new fortifications on Chechen land. The Chechen writer Abuzar Aydamirov records the founding of the Umakhan-Yurt fortification on the Sunzha river in 1837[8]. The plan of general Golovin, commander of the Separate Caucasus Corps (the head of the empire's troops in the Caucasus), for 1840 prescribed "to build a fortification at Cherkey and near old Aksai (at Gerzel-aul)" - Gerzel-aul stands on the border of Chechnya and the Kumyk plain; the construction went on all winter: the imperial historian Yurov writes that in March 1840 Pullo was personally "at Gerzel-aul to bring it into a better defensive condition", and the fortification "was finished after a fashion"[3]. |
| **[T0022 Terror September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0022Terror)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/330):** The method of the amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, was deliberately induced fear. Pullo described it plainly in a memorandum of 1840: "by threatening all the unsubmissive communities with the annihilation of their property, I instilled in them such fear, brought them to such a state, that one after another they began to submit. From 1834 to 1840 the auls of the Michik people, the Aukhovites and the Salatavians that had broken away, of Greater and Lesser Chechnya, and the never-subjugated villages of the Ichkerians and the Gumbetovians recognized the authority of the Russian government" (the listed names are highland communities of Chechnya and neighboring Dagestan)[1]. Fear was not a side effect but a declared instrument: Pullo credits the submission of the communities as the direct result of threats of annihilation. |
| **[T0077 Punitive Expeditions September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0077Punitive Expeditions)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/359):** The amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, rested on punitive sorties of the troops against the seized auls of Chechnya. Pullo described the practice in a memorandum of 1840: "I would appear unexpectedly before the astonished population of the most remote auls and, according to the degree of the village's guilt, either annihilated it or contented myself with imposing a fine, taking amanats and arresting the most guilty persons" (a fine here is a monetary penalty; amanats - hostages whom the empire took away from the auls; the "annihilation" of a village in the imperial lexicon means the destruction of its buildings and property, not of its inhabitants); auls suspected of ties with the resistance "were immediately punished with fines, with the arrest of ill-intentioned people, and in extreme cases even with the annihilation of auls"[1]. Punishment is the administrative routine of the system: the destruction of a village stands in one row with fines and arrests as a grade of punishment. |
| **[T0154 Manufacturing a Collaborating Elite September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0154Manufacturing a Collaborating Elite)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/424):** The amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, created within Chechen society a privileged layer with power over its compatriots. The offices of the overseers appointed by the empire over the auls were handed by the empire to Chechens themselves: the imperial historian Yurov writes that the pristavs "were chosen predominantly, if not exclusively, from among the militiamen" - from the highland militia, armed units of highlanders in the empire's service[3]. The historian N. I. Pokrovsky showed the mechanics of the split: the office of pristav was unpaid, so only "certain representatives of strong families" could take it, and they "took advantage of the opportunity to use their power for further accumulation"; "by creating in Chechnya a local administration, Chechen by nationality, tsarism hoped to create at the same time the Chechen 'aristocracy' it so needed"[7]. The empire gave part of the society power and privileges over the rest and bound this layer to itself, not to the people: the handing of offices to the "strong families" is documented; the calculation of growing a loyal "aristocracy" was formulated by the historian N. I. Pokrovsky. |
| **[T0155 Forced Disarmament September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0155Forced Disarmament)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/425):** The amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, included the systematic confiscation of weapons from the inhabitants of the seized auls of Chechnya. Pullo in a memorandum of 1840 called it a program of his own: "the power of the pristavs was consolidated, and at the same time a beginning was laid to the system of disarming the highlanders, by exacting from all auls one gun from every 10 saklias. In all, upward of 1900 guns were collected - a circumstance important both for the quantity of weapons collected and especially because for the first time the thought was instilled in the highlanders that the government has the right to deprive of weapons those who have used them for evil" (saklia - a highlander's house; pristav - a superintendent over the auls appointed by the empire; the figure of 1900 is Pullo's self-report; the historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov count about one and a half thousand from the archives)[1]. The historian D. A. Khozhaev writes: "The expeditions of general Pullo in December 1839 and January 1840 to uphold Russian administration, and the disarmament of the Chechen lowland auls that had begun, when Pullo demanded the surrender of one gun from every ten houses, aroused indignation in broad layers of the Chechen people"[5]. The historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov name disarmament the trigger of the uprising: "The fear that after the disarmament the authorities would introduce in Chechnya the all-Russian serfdom order, shameful for people of noble standing, which practically all Chechens considered themselves to be, made the highlanders take up arms"[6]. |
| **[T0147 Forced Registration of Subjecthood September 1836 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army (T0147Forced Registration of Subjecthood)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/417):** The amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, formalized the subordination of Chechen communities as "submission" with obligations to the empire. The 1840 register of the highland peoples, published in the documentary collection «Движение горцев северо-восточного Кавказа в 20-50 гг. XIX века», records the outcome for the Ako community (the Akintsy - a Chechen community in the upper reaches of the Gekhi river): "Declared submission in 1839, handed over amanats and pledged to pay a tribute of one silver ruble per house" (amanats - hostages whom the empire took away from the auls to control them)[1]. The formalization proceeded under the system of fear that Pullo described in a memorandum of 1840: "by threatening all the unsubmissive communities with the annihilation of their property, I instilled in them such fear... that one after another they began to submit"[1]. |

</details>

## List of Materials

1. [Гаджиев В. Г., Рамазанов X. X. Движение горцев северо-восточного Кавказа в 20-50 гг. XIX века: сборник… 1959.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/126)
2. [Гаджи-Али. Сказание очевидца о Шамиле. 1873.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/123)
3. [Юров А. 1840, 1841 и 1842-й годы на Кавказе. 1886.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/134)
4. [Кавказская археографическая комиссия. Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том IX (183… 1884.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/106)
5. [Хожаев Д. А. Чеченцы в Русско-Кавказской войне. 1998.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/95)
6. [Ахмадов Я. З., Хасмагомадов Э. Х. История Чечни в XIX-XX веках. 2005.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/125)
7. [Покровский Н. И. Кавказские войны и имамат Шамиля. 2009.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/129)
8. [Айдамиров А. А. Хронология истории Чечено-Ингушетии. 1991.](https://archive.decolonial.ist/en/127)
