posts.title: "Bombs Rained Down on the Auls": Repression and Air Strikes on Mountain Chechnya on the Eve of the Deportation (1941-1942)
posts.markdown:
# Campaign: "Bombs Rained Down on the Auls": Repression and Air Strikes on Mountain Chechnya on the Eve of the Deportation (1941-1942) (C1190)

In the autumn of 1941 the Second World War was underway: Germany was advancing on the USSR, and the front was moving toward the Caucasus. The USSR was taking Chechens to its war: during the first mass mobilization, from 29 August to 2 September 1941, the military commissariats took almost 8 thousand men - 269 managed to evade, and another 450 fled on the way to the dispatch point[1]. In October they took another 4.4 thousand - 362 did not report to the recruitment stations[1]. The commissariats sent up to 13 thousand more men, unfit for combat service, to the "labor army" - construction battalions[2]. Already in September 1941 the labor-army trains found themselves in the frontline zone, where more than 10 thousand of these men died[2]. The colonizer recorded as "deserters" those who fled death in the "labor army", those who evaded mobilization into it, and even those who failed to appear at a recruitment station because of disability or their own death; the Chechen historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The unfortunate citizens were forced either to hide from arrest or to pay bribes to the officials of the military commissariats and the NKVD" - and add: "Mass bribes taken from the highlanders became the everyday practice of the military commissariats"[2]. In early October 1941 the mountain villages of Chechnya rose against the collective farms and the mobilization - according to the report of the commander of the 141st Regiment of the NKVD Internal Troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia), Lieutenant Colonel Khalukhaev, dated 26 June 1943, the protest covered the Shatoy (Shatoevsky), Itum-Kale, Galanchozh, Cheberloy and Sharoy districts[1]. Even by the data of the secret services this was an economic protest: the population of the mountain villages "proceeded to a spontaneous division of collective-farm property" - property the colonizer had merged into collective farms during collectivization (campaign C1178); the same records charged the people with mass non-payment of taxes and evasion of mobilization; Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov likewise see "features of social protest" in the events[2]. The USSR's response was a military operation across the mountain districts, the declaration of this protest a "kulak-bandit uprising", and operational groups and NKVD troops left behind in the mountains. The historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that, "besides the operational groups and internal troops, three flights of combat aircraft were brought in" for the suppression, and "Bombs rained down on auls whose population did not even suspect any 'uprising'"[2]. "In the period from 30 October to 15 November 1941 the 141st rifle regiment, together with other units, crushed the c[ounter]-r[evolutionary] uprising in heavy multi-day fighting," Khalukhaev reported to Sheredega, head of the NKVD Internal Troops of the USSR[1].

---

<details><summary>**Procedures Carried Out (5)**</summary>

| Procedures Carried Out |
|---|
| **[T0104 Mass Killings of Civilians September 1941 C1190 "Bombs Rained Down on the Auls": Repression and Air Strikes on Mountain Chechnya on the Eve of the Deportation (1941-1942) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army (T0104Mass Killings of Civilians)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/365):** In early November 1941, waging a military operation against the "uprising" it had itself declared, the USSR bombed with combat aircraft mountain auls of Chechnya in which there was neither this invented "uprising" nor the real protest. The historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: for the suppression of the protest, "besides the operational groups and internal troops, three flights of combat aircraft were brought in," and "the operation proved poorly prepared in the military respect and was accompanied by heavy losses among the peaceful population. Bombs rained down on auls whose population did not even suspect any 'uprising'"[2]. The historian S. P. Arenin, who wrote from the documents of the NKVD Department for the Struggle against "Banditry" (a predecessor of today's FSB), writes of the operations of 28 October - 3 November 1941: they were carried out by "chekist-military groups, to which three flights of aircraft were attached"[3]. In the spring of 1942, according to memoirs, Soviet aircraft repeated the strikes on a larger scale - the Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov, who wrote about these events in emigration, testifies: "in the spring of 1942 Soviet aviation twice subjected all of mountain Checheno-Ingushetia to bombing," and "in the auls of Shatoy, Itum-Kale and Galanchozh the inhabitants killed by aerial bombing and by the Bolsheviks' artillery shelling outnumbered those left alive"[4]. Avtorkhanov adds: "In those days, when Stalin was arranging this hell over his own people, not a single German had yet set foot in the Caucasus"[4]. The report of the 141st Regiment on the military operation of 30 October - 15 November 1941 counts only its own men and "bandits" - "killed: bandits — 36... Regiment losses: killed — 6, wounded — 7"[1]; there is not a line in it about killed or wounded villagers. On the Galanchozh district the testimonies and the documents diverge: the historians cite data gathered from those who were in the mountains - that "absolute calm was observed" there, "and the bombing of peaceful auls by Soviet aviation came as a shock even to the district leadership"[2], while Khalukhaev's report names the Galanchozh district among those engulfed by the uprising[1]. |
| **[T0007 Imposition of Its Own Picture of Reality September 1941 C1190 "Bombs Rained Down on the Auls": Repression and Air Strikes on Mountain Chechnya on the Eve of the Deportation (1941-1942) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services (T0007Imposition of Its Own Picture of Reality)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/317):** The USSR declared the economic protest of the Chechens an "uprising" organized by "fascist agents". The party organs of the Soviet colonial administration of Checheno-Ingushetia, "at the prompting of the NKVD-NKGB", gave the protest of late October 1941 a name the historians render as: "an open anti-Soviet 'kulak-bandit uprising'"; the events themselves, as the historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write, bore "features of social protest"[2]. This version became fixed in the documents: in the report of the commander of the 141st Regiment of the NKVD Internal Troops, Lieutenant Colonel Khalukhaev, dated 26 June 1943, October 1941 is described thus: "an armed counter-revolutionary uprising was raised by German-fascist agents"[1]. The count kept by the secret services contradicted the picture they were imposing: over the whole of 1941 the NKVD organs eliminated 12 "bands" with a total strength of up to 100 men, recording four "bandit incidents" in which nine people died[2]. There is no uprising behind these figures: all the "bands" the NKVD counted and eliminated over the year held up to a hundred men for the whole of Chechnya, and nine people died in the clashes. The desertion the colonizer imputed to the Chechen people was the desertion of recruits, not of frontline soldiers - the certificate of Dementyev, head of the Grozny Region directorate of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, dated 1956, states: during the first mobilization "450 men deserted en route to the dispatch point, 269 men evaded the call-up"[1], and the historians confirm: the detained deserters were "by no means from the front, but from units being formed in Grozny or passing through it"[2]. On frontline desertion Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "over the first six months of the war, 38 known cases of desertion from the front line"; at the same time, they write, in Checheno-Ingushetia "they began to count as 'deserters' also those who fled death in the 'labor army' or evaded mobilization into it," and they also write about the bookkeeping: "A man was counted as an 'evader', or even a deserter, if he failed to appear at the recruitment stations at first summons, even by reason of disability or of his own death"[2]. The historians note that the assessments rested "on the data of the central apparatus of the NKVD of the ChIASSR exclusively," and that "the only real thing here was the bombing of Chechen auls and hamlets by Soviet aviation. Everything else is open to question"[2]. The military commissariats carried out three call-ups: 29 August - 2 September 1941 (8 thousand men were subject to call-up), in October 1941 (4,733 men) and on 17-25 March 1942: "14,577 men were subject to call-up, of whom only 4,395 were called up"[1] - people evaded the call-up en masse. In April 1942 the USSR cancelled the call-up of Chechens and Ingush altogether - Dementyev's certificate states: "In connection with this, in April 1942 there followed an order of the NKO of the USSR cancelling the call-up of Chechens and Ingush into the army"[1] (the NKO - the USSR ministry of defense). The Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov, writing in emigration, dates the release from service to February 1942 and renders the order's motivation in the words "the Chechens and Ingush, by religious conviction, refuse to eat pork"[4]. The historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that it was the NKVD organs that obtained the halt of the call-up in March 1942, and render the official motivation thus: "the halt of the call-up was motivated all but by care for the Chechens and Ingush, even by the impossibility of providing their nourishment with meat (the highlanders did not eat pork, and there was practically no mutton or beef laid in as canned food)"[2]. Two years later the USSR accused the people it had itself removed from the call-up of evading service and going over to the enemy; on this accusation the colonizer built the decree deporting the people from its own lands in 1944, known as Operation "Chechevitsa" ("Lentil") (campaign C1180) and later recognized as genocide of the Chechen people: by Russia in 1991[5], by the European Parliament in 2004[6] and by Ukraine in 2022[7]. |
| **[T0077 Punitive Expeditions September 1941 C1190 "Bombs Rained Down on the Auls": Repression and Air Strikes on Mountain Chechnya on the Eve of the Deportation (1941-1942) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services (T0077Punitive Expeditions)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/359):** In September 1941 the USSR created special departments for the struggle against "banditry" within the local NKVD organs, including in Chechnya, and permanent operational groups in the Shatoy, Galanchozh and Itum-Kale districts, whose task the historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov render in the words "to quickly suppress any manifestations of banditry"[2]. The first came the military operation of 30 October - 15 November 1941 across the districts of the declared "uprising": according to the report of the 141st Regiment of the NKVD Internal Troops, 36 people recorded as "bandits" were killed and 251 detained - "insurgents — 127, bandits — 7, bandit-insurgents — 13, deserters — 104"[1]. On 5 December 1941, in the village of Gikhi in the Urus-Martan district, the regiment in a two-hour battle destroyed a group of ten people that the report calls the "cadre band" of Kaidov Azak: three were killed, seven detained[1]. In the same December, to support the operational groups, the USSR formed the 178th Motorized Rifle Battalion in Chechnya, expanded the following year into the 141st Regiment of NKVD troops (in the commander's report the regiment is called a rifle regiment, by the historians - a mountain-rifle one)[2]. The regiment's count for 1941, from 25 October to 1 January 1942: 59 people killed, 390 detained[1]. |
| **[T0049 Forced Mobilization September 1941 C1190 "Bombs Rained Down on the Auls": Repression and Air Strikes on Mountain Chechnya on the Eve of the Deportation (1941-1942) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army (T0049Forced Mobilization)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/351):** In 1941 the USSR forcibly herded up to 13 thousand Chechens deemed unfit for military service into the "labor army" - construction battalions sent to build defensive lines: the people were carried toward the front without weapons and without soldier status. The mobilization, as the historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write, was carried out by the local military commissariats "by practically forcible methods"[2]; the historian M. K. Osmayev writes: "People were seized right on the streets without being served call-up papers and without preliminary explanation of the purpose of the mobilization," and among the mobilized "there were not a few old and sick men"[8]. The historians write about the position of the mobilized: they "were on the footing of servicemen but were not counted as Red Army soldiers"[2]. The historians describe the outcome: "The mobilized masses were loaded into trains and in September 1941 found themselves in the frontline zone, where no one needed their labor. The army was retreating in haste. Over 10 thousand unfortunate citizens of Checheno-Ingushetia died of cold, hunger and bombing, owing to the criminal negligence of the military officialdom"[2]. M. K. Osmayev cites another version of the fate of the mobilized: before even reaching their destination, "they were scattered by German aviation," and, by different sources, from 1,200 to 2 thousand people made it to Rostov-on-Don, whom a special commission of the colonial administration of Checheno-Ingushetia took back to Grozny[8]. The survivors the colonizer declared "deserters of the labor front"; the historians write: "They were barely saved from execution by a government commission from Checheno-Ingushetia that traveled to Rostov-on-Don in response to complaints"[2]. |
| **[T0134 Use as Cannon Fodder September 1941 C1190 "Bombs Rained Down on the Auls": Repression and Air Strikes on Mountain Chechnya on the Eve of the Deportation (1941-1942) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army (T0134Use as Cannon Fodder)](https://t.me/decolonialist_en/406):** The USSR put Chechen-Ingush volunteers into the line, but denied them weapons, supply and an army number - and on 3-4 August 1942 threw them, with sabers and miscellaneous rifles, against German tanks at Kotelnikovo. Chechens and Ingush went to fight without any imperial coercion: already in the first year of the war over 18 thousand were at the front, by the third year - 32 thousand, by other accounts up to 50 thousand[2]. After the USSR cancelled the call-up of Chechens and Ingush, Chechen-Ingush officers of the Soviet army obtained permission to recruit volunteers; their requests to arm the recruits properly, army-style, went unanswered. The Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov, who wrote about these events in emigration, names them one by one: "On the initiative of the Chechen Soviet general Supyan Mollaev, the Ingush colonel Abadiev, Major Visantov, Captain Akhtaev and others, the Soviet government permitted the Chechen-Ingush republic to recruit volunteers"[4]. Two divisions gathered, an active one and a reserve one; after the evacuation of Kerch the active division went to the Southern Front. In Krasnodar the commander of the Southern Front, Marshal Budyonny, drew it up facing the division that had retreated from Kerch and addressed the retreaters, as Avtorkhanov renders it, with these words: "Look at them, the highlanders: their fathers and grandfathers, under the leadership of the great Shamil, fought bravely for 25 years and defended their independence against the whole of tsarist Russia. Take them as your example of how to defend the Motherland!"[4]. Neither of the two divisions was taken onto the supply rolls of the Soviet army or received an army number. Avtorkhanov writes: "They were uniformed by the Chechen-Ingush republic itself, and from there they received their provisions as well"[4]. Of the fighters' weapons and footwear he writes: "the entire armament of these divisions consisted of sabers alone and of chance rifles of the most varied systems"[4]; "Many of the fighters were barefoot, as their homemade highland chuviaki had long worn out"[4]. The officers asked Budyonny to take the divisions into the army and arm them army-style. Avtorkhanov continues: "Budyonny promised to think it over. While Budyonny was thinking, the Germans crossed the Don, and the Chechen-Ingush division, in the same condition, without any support, was thrown literally under the hurricane fire of German tanks racing toward Stalingrad. At Kotelnikovo, on 4 August 1942, German tanks rolled over the corpses of many fighters of this division. A small part was taken prisoner; another, led by the staff, managed to break out of the encirclement and retreated. But the rout of this division, together with the rout of whole corps and armies of the Southern Front, served as a bad attestation for the entire Chechen-Ingush people"[4]. The historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov describe the events differently: a single 114th Chechen-Ingush Cavalry Division was being recruited - volunteers came a thousand over the establishment of 4.5 thousand - Moscow disbanded it, and the 255th Chechen-Ingush Cavalry Regiment of Major Movlid Visaitov, created on its base, was thrown by the USSR toward Stalingrad[2]. |

</details>

posts.title: Russian Empire
posts.markdown:
# Actor: Russian Empire (G0009)

The form of the state from 1721 to 1917, architects of systemic assimilation. The Russian Empire is the successor of the Tsardom of Muscovy, officially proclaimed in 1721. It is characterized by the transition to a regular state, the creation of rigid imperial institutions (the Collegia, the Senate), and the final elimination of treaty-based relations with autonomies. Within the framework, this actor focuses on the unification of governance, the erasure of administrative boundaries, and the complete absorption of local political systems through the bureaucratic apparatus.

posts.title: USSR
posts.markdown:
# Actor: USSR (G0010)

A totalitarian imperial state, officially proclaimed on December 30, 1922; de facto, a geographic expansion of the regime established by the Bolshevik party in Petrograd in October 1917. It acted as the principal actor of colonial absorption, retention, and exploitation until its collapse in 1991. While formally declaring a union of equal independent republics with the right of free secession, in practice the USSR implemented rigid unification and centralization of governance in Moscow (concentrating absolute power in the Politburo of the Central Committee). This led to the de facto elimination of the political, economic, and cultural sovereignty of the colonized nations. Within the framework, this actor is characterized by an unprecedented scale of social engineering: total control over society, the dissemination of information, the economy, and education; the use of institutional terror; the physical annihilation of the peasantry through artificial famine; mass ethnic cleansing by deporting peoples to other regions of the empire; as well as a policy of systematic Russification and the destruction/incorporation/Russification of national elites.

# Actor: Soviet Russia (RSFSR) (G0013)

A state formed as a result of the Bolshevik coup in November 1917 (official name from July 1918: the Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic). It acted as the principal actor of military expansion, hybrid war, and the colonial absorption of the Ukrainian People's Republic (UNR) in 1917–1922. In December 1922 it became a co-founder and the core part of the USSR.

# Instrument: Government (S0008)

An instrument of internal administration and institutional coercion. It comes into use once a territory has already been stripped of international subjecthood and de facto turned into an internal colony. It encompasses the work of the metropole's entire state and bureaucratic apparatus: the issuance of discriminatory laws and decrees, changes to administrative borders, systematic cultural and educational assimilation, social engineering, and the legal formalization of control (through population censuses or imitation referendums).

posts.title: Propaganda
posts.markdown:
# Instrument: Propaganda (S0021)

A state institutional apparatus of mass ideological influence, formatting of consciousness, and cognitive control. It included specialized party structures (in particular, the agitation and propaganda departments of the Central Committee), as well as the press, the system of mass events, cinema, and literature, all fully controlled by the authorities. It was used by the aggressor to replace real history with artificial imperial-communist myths, to subject the population to total ideological indoctrination, and to deliberately cultivate a fanatical totalitarian personality type, blindly devoted to the regime and cruel toward dissenters. The propaganda machine served as the basic mechanism for legitimizing state violence and masking the policy of forced assimilation.

posts.title: Police Apparatus
posts.markdown:
# Instrument: Police Apparatus (S0024)

The police apparatus provides everyday coercive and administrative control over society. The metropole needs this instrument to hold on to power, to maintain the desired order on the ground, and to keep basic records of the population, including through mechanisms of registration and restrictions on movement. From the 1600s to the present day, this system has changed only its signboards: voivode offices and investigative prikazes gave way to the city police and address bureaus in the Russian Empire. In the Soviet era, this branch of power was embodied in the vast structures of the NKVD and the MVD, and today the same supervisory and administrative function continues to be performed by the modern MVD system.

posts.title: Militarized Settlers
posts.markdown:
# Instrument: Militarized Settlers (S0025)

An instrument of demographic and military expansion that combines military service with agricultural labor and the physical settlement of territories. It is employed by the state to create an armed buffer on the frontier, to displace Indigenous populations from their lands, and to radically reduce the cost of maintaining an army of many thousands. The settlers are shifted to self-sufficiency, bound to the land, and placed under the total control of the military command. Historical incarnations: the irregular Cossack hosts (Terek, Greben, Kuban), as well as the institution of military settlements deployed on a large scale in the Russian Empire by Alexander I under the direction of Count A. A. Arakcheyev. In introducing this system, the emperor drew on European experience: the model was the Prussian cantonal system of army recruitment (Kantonssystem), under which the country was divided into military districts and a soldier's service was combined with cultivating the land, including on the territories seized after the partition of Poland.
